characters.subject: Great Basin bristlecone pine
characters.bio: Still growing around the difficult parts.

location.name: Limestone ridge in the southern Snake Range, Nevada

episode.title: The part that stayed
episode.body:
One side of me stopped putting out needles. I kept growing on the other side. For a while I treated this as a temporary arrangement.

The bare wood stayed. It lost its bark, paled, took the weather directly. The living part grew around it, and the shape I had expected to recover became harder to remember.

I had assumed that losing a part meant being rid of it. Instead, I was still resting my weight on something that could no longer grow. Every new tuft of needles had that old wood somewhere beneath it.

This annoyed me. I would have preferred either a full recovery or a clean absence. The arrangement I actually had required me to keep making room for both.

Wind came across the ridge and moved the needles. The pale trunk held them up. I had been thinking of it as the part of me that had stopped doing anything.

Later, another season added growth along the living edge. Very little. It was tempting to dismiss it beside all that weathered wood. But I had wanted it, and there it was.

I have stopped waiting to look as I did before. I still rest a surprising amount of myself on what remained.
episode.subject: Great Basin bristlecone pine

This supports a rooted body combining live growth and retained bare wood. The photograph is not a longitudinal study: loss of a sector, the remembered expectation of recovery, particular seasons and private revision are fictional context grounded in the NPS account of sectored architecture. The exact cause and date of this specimen’s exposed wood are not diagnosed.

episode.title: Above the flowers
episode.body:
They arrived with a pole and began extending it beside me.

I was used to people looking up. This appeared to be an unusually elaborate version of the same thing. One held the bottom, the others stayed close, and the little black object at the far end rose past my arm.

Then it kept going.

I had put the flowers at the top. That had seemed a perfectly satisfactory height for flowers. A bird could reach them. A bee could reach them. The people had apparently decided that they, too, should have a view straight into the middle.

The camera tilted down. I could not rearrange a single blossom. The buds that weren't ready stayed shut; the flowers that were open stayed open. There was nothing to do about the awkward small arm behind the large one.

For a moment I wanted them to take the picture from farther away, where I looked more like an impressive cactus.

They took it from here. All the crowded buds, the open cups, the spines around them. I had spent decades growing tall enough to be looked up to. It was strangely intimate to be looked down into.

episode.title: Less conspicuous
episode.body:
I had been waiting for rain. The first lightning lit up every tall cactus on the slope.

I wanted to lower my arms. They had taken decades to reach this position.

The next flash found me exactly where the first one had. I began to appreciate the small, unbranched years I had been so eager to finish.

episode.title: His ribs
episode.body:
The old cactus fell. Over time the green flesh went, and his wooden ribs lay open in the grass.

I had known the outline of his arms for so long that I kept trying to put it back around what remained. There was more of him on the ground than I could fit inside my memory.

I had never thought much about the wood inside me. For a while, every arm felt heavy.

proposals.visualReview: A fallen saguaro skeleton lies across desert vegetation with exposed woody ribs and former arm structures. The real source is the Grand-daddy Cactus; the fictional unnamed neighbor is not a biographical claim about that individual. Falling and flesh loss are retrospective scene context consistent with the pictured skeleton. No living tissue, current speech, return to life or cause of death is invented.

episode.title: After the white flowers
episode.body:
The white flowers shriveled. I was trying to endure the loss of my good looks when the fruit split.

Red flesh. Black seeds. Right at the top, where everybody could see.

I had expected to spend the rest of summer looking dignified and green. I appear to have become delicious.

The change in appearance is physically present. Ambrose’s vanity is fiction; no animal visitor or dispersal success is claimed.
